summary: Discusses problems with NAT-PT, the IPv6-to-IPv4 translation mechanism defined in RFC 2766. The problems are serious enough that it should no longer be recommended as a general transition tool, and the document recommends reclassifying RFC 2766 as Historic. It is informational.

eli5.summary: An old translator between two internet languages had too many problems, so this says to stop recommending it.

subtitle: Why the IETF concluded that NAT-PT should no longer be recommended as a way to connect IPv6-only and IPv4-only hosts.

tldr.problem: RFC 2766 defined NAT-PT, a translator that lets IPv6-only and IPv4-only nodes talk to each other during the move to IPv6. Experience and earlier documents raised many problems with it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects those issues in three groups: those unrelated to the DNS application layer gateway (DNS-ALG), those made worse by it, and those caused directly by it. It then weighs the effect on IPv6 application development.
tldr.outcome: The issues are judged serious enough that NAT-PT should not be recommended as a general transition mechanism, and RFC 2766 should be moved from Proposed Standard to Historic status.

facts.label: Recommends moving
facts.value: RFC 2766 from Proposed Standard to Historic

today: RFC 4966 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 2766, the NAT-PT specification it recommends retiring. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What NAT-PT Is and Why Review It
sections.content:
RFC 2766 defines NAT-PT (Network Address Translator - Protocol Translator), a set of network-layer translation mechanisms meant to let IPv4-only nodes communicate with IPv6-only nodes during the transition to IPv6. Basic NAT-PT translates only addresses. NAPT-PT also translates transport identifiers, which saves scarce IPv4 addresses. Packet translation itself uses the SIIT algorithm from RFC 2765.

This document summarizes issues raised in earlier documents, adds issues carried over from traditional IPv4 NATs, and identifies a few new ones. Most of the earlier documents are unlikely to become RFCs, so the issues are summarized here.

The RFC treats the DNS application layer gateway (DNS-ALG) as an integral part of NAT-PT. RFC 2766 is ambiguous on this point, but the 'simple' case without a DNS-ALG was never worked out. Issues that do not depend on the DNS-ALG apply to any network-layer translator, including ones based on SIIT.
sections.eli5: NAT-PT was a go-between that let computers speaking two different internet languages talk. This paper lists everything that went wrong with it.

sections.title: Issues Independent of the DNS-ALG
sections.content:
These issues apply to any IPv6-IPv4 translator.

  • Embedded addresses. Protocols that carry IP addresses in their payloads need a helper (an ALG) for each protocol, and these protocols keep evolving. IPv6 and IPv4 addresses differ in length, so packet lengths change too. IPsec AH, and ESP in transport mode, cannot pass through NAT-PT unless UDP encapsulation is used, without ending the security association at the translator.
  • Redirection. A port translator needs something like a port number to pick the right binding. Protocols such as RSVP, which run directly over IP, may lack it.
  • Binding decay. Bindings are soft state and time out, so applications must send keepalives during long idle periods. RFC 2766 does not say how to choose timeouts.
  • Lost information. IPv4 has no equivalent of the IPv6 flow label, some IPv6 extension headers (routing headers, mobility extensions) cannot be translated, and some ICMP messages have no counterpart.
  • Fragmentation. Fragments after the first carry no port numbers, so a NAPT-PT cannot translate them. Workarounds cost state, memory and delay, and open the door to fragment-based denial of service.

Further issues concern SCTP multihoming, Mobile IPv6 route optimization, which a translator cannot pass to an IPv4 node, and multicast, which SIIT cannot translate.
sections.eli5: A translator that rewrites the address on every letter breaks any letter that also has the address written inside it. It also loses things that have no word in the other language, and it forgets who is who if you stay quiet too long.

sections.title: Issues Made Worse by the DNS-ALG
sections.content:
NAT-PT depends on its DNS-ALG to hand out the translated addresses that hosts use. That has consequences for how a network is built.

  • Topology. The NAT-PT must sit on the path of the DNS queries, which effectively makes it the default IPv6 router for the site. On sites with dual-stack nodes, all traffic then flows through it.
  • Scalability and failure. Like traditional NAT, it is a bottleneck and, because flows are anchored to one box, a single point of failure. Clusters of cooperating boxes need state synchronization that has not been standardized.
  • No address persistence. Mappings made through DNS can expire before use, and applications that need the same mapping across sessions may break.
  • Denial of service. NAT-PT specifies no authentication, so spoofed packets or plain DNS queries can create bindings and exhaust memory and address or port pools. Address spoofing is not needed for the DNS-based attack.

The proposed workarounds, such as separate DNS servers for IPv6-only clients, only partly help, and an alternate suggestion is judged flawed because a client cannot know in advance which DNS server to ask.
sections.eli5: Because everything has to go through one translator, it becomes crowded, it is a single weak spot, and a prankster can keep asking it questions until it runs out of room.

sections.title: Issues Caused by the DNS-ALG
sections.content:
Some problems come directly from how the DNS-ALG rewrites DNS answers.

  • Address selection. For a dual-stack host the DNS-ALG returns both native IPv6 and translated IPv4 addresses as AAAA records, and address selection under RFC 3484 can always prefer the translated one. Applications also cannot tell that an IPv6 address is really a translated IPv4 one.
  • Non-global records. Translated records are only usable through the translating NAT-PT, which breaks the DNS expectation that answers are consistent for any user.
  • Wrong answers to A queries. The DNS-ALG is stateless, so it can wrongly turn the answer to an A query into a translated AAAA record.
  • Multi-addressed nodes. The DNS-ALG must translate every address of a host, so many bindings are created.
  • DNSSEC. Rewriting responses invalidates DNSSEC signatures, so DNSSEC is not deployable in domains that use NAT-PT as specified.
sections.eli5: The translator also rewrites the phone book answers, so a host can be handed an address that only works through that translator, and secret-seal checks on the answers stop working.

sections.title: Effect on IPv6 Applications
sections.content:
IPv6 is meant to restore end-to-end transparency, so developers may skip the NAT traversal measures they use on IPv4. NAT-PT is designed to be transparent to applications, so they have no way to discover it on a path. Applications that assume a NAT-free IPv6 network may break behind it, and it is likely to inhibit the use of additional IPv6 capabilities such as the flexible extension header system.

Making applications detect and work around a temporary transition aid is described as a very bad idea, since their behavior would then differ between native IPv6 and NAT-PT environments.
sections.eli5: A hidden translator in the middle means programs cannot know it is there, so they can fail in surprising ways. It is a bad deal to make every program plan for a stopgap.

sections.title: Conclusion and Recommendation
sections.content:
Some issues have proposed fixes, but those need major changes to the specification and more operational complexity, and NAT-PT would still have irresolvable issues and limited applicability. At the time, 3GPP networks were the only standardised scenario where NAT-PT was envisaged, and RFC 4215 recommends against the generic form and suggests application proxies as an alternative.

The RFC does not rule out all translation. A more limited translator could be defined for constrained situations. It recommends that the IETF no longer suggest NAT-PT as a general IPv4-IPv6 transition mechanism, and that RFC 2766 be moved to Historic status to limit inappropriate deployment.
sections.eli5: The authors say: stop recommending this go-between, retire its rulebook, and if we need a translator later, build a smaller and better one.

items.title: Independent of the DNS-ALG
items.text: Embedded addresses, redirection, binding decay, lost information, fragmentation, SCTP, mobility, multicast.

items.title: Exacerbated by the DNS-ALG
items.text: Topology constraints, scalability, lack of address persistence, denial of service.

items.title: Caused by the DNS-ALG
items.text: Address selection, non-global records, wrong A-query answers, multi-addressed nodes, DNSSEC.
